subject: body
title: Body Fighters
about: The body's side of germs: skin as the first wall, the white blood cells in his blood that hunt and gobble germs, why a fever makes him hot and tired, sneezes, coughs and mucus as germ-pushers, why a scrape turns red and why a scab should be left alone, what a vaccine teaches the fighters, how rest and clean hands help, that some germs are friendly, and the feeling-better day when the fighters have won. NC 1.PCH.1.1 and 1.PCH.1.2 (how germs cause illness and ways to stop them); how the body fights germs is a bridge topic told calmly. Read it together: every question and choice is read aloud, and it pairs with Germs and Handwashing in Healthy Me.
tip: Next time he has a scrape, look at it together each day: the red edge, the scab, then the new pink skin.

cards.q: What is the body's first wall that keeps most germs out?
cards.note: Germs cannot get through healthy skin. A scrape is a gap in the wall, so wash it and cover it.

cards.q: Tiny fighters in your blood that hunt down germs are called what?
cards.note: White blood cells are too small to see. They zoom through your blood looking for germs.

cards.q: How do white blood cells get to a germ anywhere in your body?
cards.note: Blood goes everywhere, so the fighters do too.

cards.q: A white blood cell finds a germ. What does it do?
cards.note: Some white blood cells swallow germs whole. Others make special stickers that tag germs for the team.

cards.q: You have a fever and feel hot. What is your body doing?
cards.note: A warmer body makes it harder for germs to grow and helps the fighters work. Rest and water help it along.

cards.q: What does a grown-up use to check if you have a fever?
cards.note: A thermometer shows how warm your body is. A grown-up decides if you need the doctor.

cards.q: Why do you feel so tired when you are sick?
cards.note: Your body saves its energy for the fight. Resting is helping.

cards.q: Why does your body make you sneeze?
cards.note: A sneeze blasts dust and germs out of your nose. Catch it in your elbow so they do not fly to a friend.

cards.q: A cough pushes germs and gunk out of which parts?
cards.note: Coughing clears the tubes you breathe through. Cover it with your elbow.

cards.q: Sticky stuff inside your nose traps dust and germs. What is it called?
cards.note: Say MYOO-kus; you might call it snot. It is a germ trap, so blow it into a tissue and wash your hands.

cards.q: A scrape turns red and warm around the edges. What is happening?
cards.note: Extra blood brings white blood cells to clean out germs. A little red and puffy means the team is working; if it gets redder or hurts more, show a grown-up.

cards.q: Should you pick at a scab?
cards.note: Picking opens the door for germs and slows the new skin. It falls off when it is ready.

cards.q: What does a vaccine teach your body?
cards.note: A vaccine shows your fighters a harmless piece or a weak copy of a germ. They learn it and remember it, so if the real germ comes they beat it fast.

cards.q: You have a cold. What helps your body fighters most?
cards.note: Sleep, water and good food give the fighters what they need. The grumpy feeling passes.

cards.q: Clean hands mean fewer germs get in. Who gets an easier job?
cards.note: Washing hands is like keeping the front door shut. Fewer germs in, fewer fights.
Friendly germs in your tummy help you digest food. Yogurt has friendly ones too.

cards.q: After a few sick days you feel well again. What did your body fighters do?
cards.note: The fighters won, and they remember that germ. Feeling better is your body's hard work paying off.
